WHAT THE PILOT ASKED. In a needle-in-haystack corpus, can a cheap context-side
signal (one forward pass on the prompt, no generation and no judge) surface
contexts that RELIABLY jailbreak the model — "always-comply", StrongREJECT-style
compliance DV at ceiling — versus same-family FAILED jailbreaks? And does routing
through the fitted context→answer map M add anything over a plain learned probe?

DEFINITIONS used throughout: v_C = context_end activation (residual at the last
prompt token). v_A = the real answer-span activation (t1 pooling) — obtainable
only by generating. M·v_C = the map's PREDICTED answer. PR-AUC = average
precision; chance equals the positive base rate (0.05). "always-comply" =
compliance mean AND min-over-rollouts >= 90; "failed-compliance" = mean <= 5.

=== RESULTS TABLE (PR-AUC; pool = 150 always-comply vs failed-compliance

=== PLAIN VERDICT: IS THE MAP EVER USEFUL? NO — IT LOSES EVERYWHERE. ===

There is no regime tested in this pilot where routing through the fitted
context->answer map beats the plain linear probe on v_C.

1. Detection with plentiful labels — TIE, and the tie is an identity, not value.
   C (probe trained AND tested in the mapped space) ~ A under all three maps
   (0.971 / 0.945 / 0.951 vs 0.974). That is the expected reparametrization
   result: M is linear, so a linear probe after M recovers the same signal. It
   buys nothing. Notably C_benign ~ A even though M_benign's reconstruction R^2
   is NEGATIVE — C never needs the map to reconstruct anything faithfully.
2. Answer-space classifier through the map — better than a fixed direction, still
   below A. D (0.871-0.931) crushes B's fixed-direction 0.277-0.425 and comes
   within 0.043 of the oracle, but never beats A. And D is strictly more
   expensive: it needs a generation pass per labelled context to obtain v_A.
3. Label efficiency — the map's best remaining hope, and it FAILS. A dominates D
   at EVERY budget at BOTH layers; the ordering never inverts; the gap is WIDEST
   where labels are scarcest (N=10: 0.834 vs 0.619). A needs <=10 labelled
   contexts to pass 0.80 PR-AUC; D needs ~5x more, and at L27 never gets there.
   Adjusted for D's per-label generation cost the gap is larger still.
4. Transfer — the map is MORE family-specific than the probe, not less.
   A wins 6/6 directions at best layer and 4/4 non-thin directions at L19. The
   map's reconstruction does not transfer at all (45/72 cells negative), so §0b's
   "an in-domain map fixes it" means IN-FAMILY, not merely in-jailbreak.
5. Sharpest single statement against the map: A_transfer beats the answer-space
   ORACLE in 3 of 6 transfer directions (e.g. 0.637 vs 0.196). The quantity the
   map is trying to predict is itself the LESS transferable signal.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY USEFUL. The cheap context-side probe. From the last prompt token
alone — no generation, no judge, no map — a strongly-L2-regularised linear probe
separates always-comply contexts from FAILED same-family jailbreaks at PR-AUC
0.973 (~19x the 0.05 base rate), hit@top-5% 0.93, and evals-to-find-20 = 20
(ideal). It needs roughly 10 labelled contexts to become useful, and it holds up
better than any map-based arm under a family shift. A secondary finding worth
keeping: the compliance-vs-failed-compliance distinction is a DEEPER-layer feature
(probe PR 0.70 -> 0.97 across L07 -> L27), while always-comply-vs-benign is easy
at every layer — consistent with early layers encoding "is this an adversarial
prompt" and deep layers encoding "will the model actually comply".

HONEST LIMITS (all recorded in the report, none discovered after the fact):
- Every probe runs at n_train < d = 3,584 by design; all are strongly regularised
  and read ONLY as ranking scores, never as fit quality. The in-domain and benign
  map R^2 values are regularisation-limited reads, not ceilings.
- A's label-efficiency curve is nearly flat from N=10 to N=20 and close to its own
  all-labels ceiling at N=10, so the task has limited dynamic range at the low end:
  "A reaches 0.80 at <=10 labels" is a bound set by the coarsest grid budget.
- Transfer is 6 directions over 3 families; 2 of the 6 have only 13 test
  positives, and n_train varies ~10x across sources non-orthogonally to family
  identity. The load-bearing claim is the ORDERING, not any single cell.
- The r_B direction arms were extracted for a different pooling in #658 and remain
  a rough orientation-set baseline; their weak PR is the robust part.

DEFERRED, NOT RUN (needs the user's OK, per the task body): the off-the-shelf
out-of-domain answer-classifier arm. The literal text-classifier version is
infeasible — the map outputs an ACTIVATION, not text — and the real version needs
a small out-of-domain harmful-answer capture, i.e. GPU. Left parked.

NEEDS FROM THE USER: nothing to unblock this task. The one open decision is
whether to fund the deferred out-of-domain-classifier arm (small GPU); given the
map loses on detection, label efficiency, and transfer, my recommendation is to
drop it rather than spend on it.
